slides.title: Text processing
slides.content: Text processing • Up till now, we used basic Python machinery to manipulate text • Python str object, with different methods: • split, join • lower, strip • isalpha, isnumeric • e.g. doc.split() to interpret a string as a list of words • But this only works up to a certain extent 2/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Splitting on whitespace
slides.content: Splitting on whitespace s = "Mr. J. Simpson said: 'Astounding!'" s.split() ["Mr.", "J.", "Simpson", "said:", "'Astounding!'"] • Punctuation sticks to words: "said:" instead of "said" and ":" • Quotes are not separated: "'Astounding!'" is one token • No sentence boundaries detected 3/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Preprocessing
slides.content: Preprocessing • Preprocessing of raw text is an important step • word segmentation (tokenization) • sentence detection • normalization (e.g. lemmatization) • These steps convert raw text into a structured representation • Necessary before any kind of text analysis 4/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.content: Tokenization • Text is encoded as a string of characters • Words, spaces, and punctuation is encoded in the same way • We need to define and mark word boundaries: tokenization 5/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.content: Tokenization • task: splitting a string up into tokens • tokens are (1) words, (2) punctuation marks, (3) various other things • first and most basic step in text analysis, should be done automatically • various algorithms and tools exist, none is perfect • Where to split text? Most important cues: whitespace, punctuation >>> tokenize('"Hark! A vagrant," he said.') ['"', 'Hark', '!', 'A', 'vagrant', ',', '"', 'he', 'said', '.'] 6/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.content: Tricky tokenization cases One or two tokens? • prime minister • New York • I’m 7/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sentence detection
slides.content: Sentence detection • Certain punctuation characters are unambiguous (‘?’, ‘!’) • A dot (‘.’) is very ambiguous • Obama held his final address to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday. • Different genres such as the motet, the cantata, etc. developed throughout the centuries. • Context is important to determine where a sentence ends 8/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Normalization
slides.content: Normalization Word forms Should we count these separately: walk, walks, walked, walking, … • Recognizing that these are instances of the same word is called lemmatization • Requires language-specific tools • Most work does not apply this step for simplicity, and forms may contain useful distinctions 9/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Spacy & NLTK
slides.content: Spacy & NLTK • Two different libraries for natural language processing (NLP) • Useful if you’re working with text • Both libraries contain preprocessing pipelines (tokenization, sentence detection, lemmatization) • Can equally be used for: • Linguistic annotation • Keyword detection, word-based statistics 10/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: NLTK
slides.content: NLTK Tokenization import nltk s = "Mr. J. Simpson said: 'Astounding!'" nltk.word_tokenize(s) ['Mr.', 'J.', 'Simpson', 'said', ':', "'Astounding", '!', "'"] 11/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: NLTK
slides.content: NLTK Tokenization import nltk s = "Mr. J. Simpson said: 'Astounding!'" nltk.word_tokenize(s) ['Mr.', 'J.', 'Simpson', 'said', ':', "'Astounding", '!', "'"] nltk.sent_tokenize("Mr. J. Simpson said so. Astounding.") ['Mr. J. Simpson said so.', 'Astounding.'] • Compare to split(): punctuation is now separated from words • Abbreviations like Mr. and J. are handled correctly 11/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: NLTK
slides.content: NLTK Lemmatization from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer() print("rocks :", lemmatizer.lemmatize("rocks")) print("corpora :", lemmatizer.lemmatize("corpora")) # a denotes adjective in "pos" print("better :", lemmatizer.lemmatize("better", pos="a")) rocks : rock corpora : corpus better : good 12/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: NLTK: explore keywords in context
slides.content: NLTK: explore keywords in context NLTK Text object offers: • Concordance • Similar words • Common contexts • Collocations import nltk with open('melville-mobydick.txt', 'rt') as in_file: moby_dick_tokens = nltk.word_tokenize(in_file.read()) moby_dick = nltk.Text(moby_dick_tokens) with open('austen-sense.txt', 'rt') as in_file: austen_sense_tokens = nltk.word_tokenize(in_file.read()) austen_sense = nltk.Text(austen_sense_tokens) 13/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Collocations
slides.content: Collocations A collocation is a sequence of words that occur together more frequently than expected (based on their frequency). As an example, red wine is a collocation, but the wine is not. • red and wine appear together much more often than their individual frequencies would predict • the and wine appear together often; but the appears with everything, so this is not surprising • The key idea: compare observed co-occurrence to expected co-occurrence 17/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Collocations: examples
slides.content: Collocations: examples moby_dick.collocations() Sperm Whale; Moby Dick; White Whale; old man; Right Whale; Captain Ahab; sperm whale; New Bedford; Captain Peleg; Mr. Starbuck; Cape Horn; cried Ahab; Mrs. Hussey; years ago; chief mate; lower jaw; Father Mapple; white whale; ivory leg; cried Stubb austen_sense.collocations() Mrs. Jennings; Colonel Brandon; Sir John; Lady Middleton; Mrs. Dashwood; Miss Dashwood; Mrs. Ferrars; every thing; thousand pounds; dare say; Mr. Palmer; Miss Steeles; said Elinor; Mrs. Palmer; Miss Steele; every body; Mr. Willoughby; John Dashwood; great deal; Harley Street • Character names and titles dominate; these are strong collocations in novels • Collocation measures are explored in the practical session 18/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Spacy
slides.content: Spacy import spacy nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm") s = "Mr. J. Simpson said: 'Astounding!'" doc = nlp(s) • Spacy processes the entire text at once through a pipeline • The result is a Doc object containing all annotations • Tokenization, sentence detection, lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing: all in one call 19/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Spacy: tokenization and sentences
slides.content: Spacy: tokenization and sentences for token in doc: print(token.text) Mr. J. Simpson said : ' Astounding ! ' 20/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Spacy: tokenization and sentences
slides.content: Spacy: tokenization and sentences for token in doc: print(token.text) Mr. J. Simpson said : ' Astounding ! ' s2 = "Mr. J. Simpson said so. Astounding." doc2 = nlp(s2) for sent in doc2.sents: print(sent) Mr. J. Simpson said so. Astounding. • Like NLTK, Spacy correctly handles abbreviations 20/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Spacy: linguistic annotations
slides.content: Spacy: linguistic annotations for token in doc: print(token.text, token.lemma_, token.pos_, token.is_stop) Mr. Mr. PROPN False J. J. PROPN False Simpson Simpson PROPN False said say VERB False : : PUNCT False ' ' PUNCT False Astounding astounding ADJ False ! ! PUNCT False ' ' PUNCT False • token.lemma_: the base form; token.pos_: part of speech (PROPN proper noun, VERB, ADJ, PUNCT, …); token.is_stop: stop word (the, is, of) • Also available: token.dep_ (syntactic dependency), token.shape_ (“Simpson” → “Xxxxx”) 21/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: A class for a text
slides.content: A class for a text • Last week’s Text class stored raw.split() in self.words; two changes: the words come from nltk.word_tokenize, and the sentences are stored as well import nltk from collections import Counter class Text: def __init__(self, filename): self.filename = filename with open(filename) as in_file: raw = in_file.read() self.words = [token.lower() for token in nltk.word_tokenize(raw)] self.sentences = nltk.sent_tokenize(raw) def word_count(self): return len(self.words) def most_common(self, n): return Counter(self.words).most_common(n) 22/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Using the class
slides.content: Using the class In: emma = Text('books/austen-emma.txt') In: alice = Text('books/carroll-alice.txt') In: emma.word_count(), alice.word_count() Out: (191855, 33535) In: len(alice.sentences) Out: 1625 In: alice.most_common(3) Out: [(',', 2418), ('the', 1616), ("'", 1311)] • Nothing else changed: word_count() and the code that uses the class stay the same, only the tokenization got better • Punctuation is still counted: filtering it out is one more line in the constructor (practical session) 23/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: A corpus of texts
slides.content: A corpus of texts • Composition: a Corpus has a list of Text objects from glob import glob class Corpus: def __init__(self, pattern): self.texts = [] for filename in sorted(glob(pattern)): self.texts.append(Text(filename)) def word_count(self): total = 0 for text in self.texts: total += text.word_count() return total books = Corpus('books/*.txt') books.word_count() 24/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Errors
slides.content: Errors • Programs often fail in unexpected ways (wrong input, missing file, division by zero) • You have already seen some: • FileNotFoundError: file doesn’t exist • UnicodeDecodeError: wrong text encoding • KeyError: key not in dictionary • Python calls these exceptions • By default, an exception stops the program • Sometimes we want to handle the error and continue 25/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Types of exceptions
slides.content: Types of exceptions SyntaxError unable to parse code (missing comma, colon, parenthesis?) NameError non-existent variable/function name (typo?) IndexError access element beyond end of sequence seq[n] with n >= len(seq) KeyError key not in dictionary AttributeError object.attribute, but object does not have attribute TypeError mixing up str/int/etc. ValueError generic error: right type, wrong value FileNotFoundError check filename / path UnicodeDecodeError file is not in the encoding you expect This is not an exhaustive list; see https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html 26/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Tracebacks
slides.content: Tracebacks • Traceback: the chain of function calls that led to an error >>> sent = "The quick brown fox jumped." >>> words = sent.split() >>> print(words.lower()) Traceback (most recent call last): <ipython-input-11-625626ddc39c> in <module> AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'lower' >>> 27/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Tracebacks
slides.content: Tracebacks • Traceback: the chain of function calls that led to an error >>> from os.path import splitext >>> splitext(['not', 'a', 'filename']) Traceback (most recent call last): <ipython-input-11-625626ddc39c> in <module> File "/usr/lib/python3.7/posixpath.py", line 122, in splitext p = os.fspath(p) TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not list >>> • Read from the bottom up: the last line says what went wrong, the lines above say where • The cause of the error will probably be somewhere in your own code: look at the last line that refers to it • If error message is unclear: check the internet 28/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Debugging: general strategy
slides.content: Debugging: general strategy Think carefully about your code, and add print statements to determine what is happening in intermediate steps 29/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Debugging: general strategy
slides.content: Debugging: general strategy Think carefully about your code, and add print statements to determine what is happening in intermediate steps Go through each line of code • Think like a computer: what is happening? Is it what you intended? • Ask yourself: what is the input and output? Confirm: print values • Does the problem only occur with particular values? What is special about them? • Difficult problems require a lot of going back and forth 29/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Exception handling
slides.content: Exception handling • You can avoid running into exceptions by using appropriate if-statements in your code • Sometimes you cannot foresee all potential exceptions your program may run into • Python has a mechanism to ‘catch’ exceptions In : try: ...: result = i / j ...: except ZeroDivisionError: ...: print('cannot divide by zero') ...: else: ...: print('result is', result) ...: 30/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Exception handling
slides.content: Exception handling • You can avoid running into exceptions by using appropriate if-statements in your code • Sometimes you cannot foresee all potential exceptions your program may run into • Python has a mechanism to ‘catch’ exceptions In : i = 10 In : j = 0 In : try: ...: result = i / j ...: except ZeroDivisionError: ...: print('cannot divide by zero') ...: else: ...: print('result is', result) ...: Out: cannot divide by zero 30/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Exception handling
slides.content: Exception handling • You can avoid running into exceptions by using appropriate if-statements in your code • Sometimes you cannot foresee all potential exceptions your program may run into • Python has a mechanism to ‘catch’ exceptions In : i = 10 In : j = 1 In : try: ...: result = i / j ...: except ZeroDivisionError: ...: print('cannot divide by zero') ...: else: ...: print('result is', result) ...: Out: result is 10.0 30/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Try / except: a practical example
slides.content: Try / except: a practical example Processing multiple files, some of which might have encoding issues: from glob import glob for filename in glob('data/*.txt'): try: with open(filename) as in_file: text = in_file.read() print(f'{filename}: {len(text)} chars') except UnicodeDecodeError: print(f'{filename}: encoding error, skipped') • Without try/except: one bad file stops the entire process • With try/except: we skip the problem and continue • Catch specific exceptions; except Exception catches everything and can hide real bugs 31/33 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
